title: Procurement Management
tagline: Buy smarter, source fairly and protect every rupee: practical procurement from purchase request to supplier performance, for Pakistan's organisations.
sectors: Government departments and public sector companies
description:
Procurement decides where a large share of every organisation's money goes. Done well, it lowers costs, secures supply and keeps the organisation clean. Done badly, it leaks cash through unmanaged spend, weak contracts, cosy supplier deals and outright fraud. This certification gives procurement and supply-chain professionals the tools to do it well.

You will follow the **procure-to-pay cycle** from need to payment, write specifications that invite competition, run **spend analysis** and position categories on the **Kraljic matrix**, and design sourcing events using **RFI, RFQ and RFP**, weighted scoring, two-stage and two-envelope methods. You will see how **public procurement in Pakistan** under the PPRA framework differs from private-sector practice, and calculate **total cost of ownership** instead of chasing the lowest price.

The second half is about winning and keeping value: negotiation with **BATNA, ZOPA and anchoring**, contracts with sound clauses, **Incoterms**, SLAs and liquidated damages, supplier performance management, and the risks every buyer must spot: single sourcing, conflicts of interest, bid rigging and invoice fraud. You finish with ethics, sustainable procurement, e-procurement and the KPIs that prove procurement's value.

Five stages, a ten-question test after each, and a tough timed final exam built on realistic Pakistani scenarios and real calculations.
audience: Procurement officers, buyers and purchase executives in private companies
Procurement and supply-chain managers who run tenders, contracts and supplier panels
Procurement staff in government departments, autonomous bodies and public sector companies
Finance, audit and internal control staff who review purchasing and payments
Plant, project and department managers who raise requirements and sit on evaluation committees
NGO and development-programme staff who buy under donor or public rules
outcomes: Map the procure-to-pay cycle, write sound specifications and apply three-way matching and approval controls
Analyse spend and position categories on the Kraljic matrix to choose the right sourcing strategy
Design and evaluate RFQ and RFP events using clear criteria, weighted scoring and the right tendering method
Explain how Pakistan's public procurement framework differs from private practice and calculate total cost of ownership
Prepare and conduct negotiations using BATNA, ZOPA and anchoring, and draft contracts with sound clauses, Incoterms, SLAs and liquidated damages
Manage supplier performance and recognise single-source, fraud, conflict-of-interest and bid-rigging risks
Apply ethical, sustainable and digital procurement practice and report value with the right KPIs

quest.name: Twelve Weeks to Launch
quest.premise: You have just joined the procurement team of Noor Valley Foods, a fast-growing Lahore dairy and juice company. Its new UHT plant in Sheikhupura must start production in twelve weeks, but spend is leaking, the main packaging-film supplier is raising prices and somebody seems to be gaming the tenders. With CPO Farah Qureshi as your mentor, buyer Bilal Akhtar, finance partner Zainab Khokhar and plant manager Tariq Mehmood, clear five stages to launch the plant on time and on budget, then face the final boss: the board's procurement review.

badge.name: Value Guardian
badge.description: Awarded to procurement professionals who source fairly, buy on total value, contract tightly and keep every rupee clean.

sessions.title: The Procure-to-Pay Cycle, Specifications and Spend Analysis
sessions.summary: Before you can buy better, you need to see how buying really happens: the procure-to-pay cycle and its controls, how needs become specifications, how spend analysis turns messy data into insight, and how the Kraljic matrix tells you which strategy each category deserves.
objectives: Describe the procure-to-pay cycle and the controls at each step, including three-way matching and segregation of duties
Challenge a need and write a specification that is clear, measurable and open to competition
Run the main steps of a spend analysis and read its results, including the Pareto pattern
Position categories on the Kraljic matrix and choose a fitting strategy for each quadrant

cards.title: Day one: twelve weeks on the clock
cards.setting: Procurement floor, Noor Valley Foods head office, Gulberg, Lahore. 9:10 am.

lines.text: A countdown is scrawled on the whiteboard: 12 WEEKS TO SHEIKHUPURA START-UP. Under it, a pile of invoices held together with a bulldog clip.
Welcome. I am Farah Qureshi, CPO. Before you buy anything for the new plant, look at this pile. Every one of these invoices arrived with no purchase order behind it.
Zainab, finance. Last year about a fifth of our spend went out like this. I cannot tell you what we bought, from whom, or whether we paid the agreed price.
(on WhatsApp voice note) Farah sahiba, Tariq from Sheikhupura. I need the Italian filler valves, the exact brand I used at my last plant. No substitutes, please, and I need them yesterday.
Bilal, senior buyer. And our biggest spend line, packaging film, comes from one supplier: Kohsar Flexpack. Imran Butt's company.
So, stage one: the Paper Maze. Learn how buying should flow, how needs become specs, and what our spend data is really telling us. Then we decide where to fight first.

cards.title: From need to payment in six moves

scenes.heading: A need appears
scenes.narration: Every purchase starts with a need. A plant needs valves, an office needs laptops. The first job is to confirm the need is real and cannot be met from existing stock.

scenes.heading: Requisition and approval
scenes.narration: The user raises a purchase requisition. A manager with the right approval authority signs it off, which confirms the budget and the business case.

scenes.heading: Sourcing
scenes.narration: Procurement finds the right supplier: from an existing contract, through quotations, or through a full tender for bigger or riskier buys.

scenes.heading: The purchase order
scenes.narration: A purchase order goes to the supplier before anything is delivered. It fixes what is bought, the price, quantity, delivery and terms. It is the organisation's commitment.

scenes.heading: Receipt and invoice
scenes.narration: Stores checks the delivery and records a goods received note. The supplier sends an invoice. Accounts compares the order, the receipt and the invoice: the three-way match.

scenes.heading: Payment and records
scenes.narration: Only a matched invoice is paid, on the agreed terms. Everything is filed so auditors, and you, can trace each rupee back to a genuine need.

cards.title: The procure-to-pay cycle
cards.caption: It is a cycle: payment and performance data feed back into the next need, the next specification and the next sourcing decision.

items.label: Need and requisition
items.detail: Confirm the need, check stock, raise a requisition with budget code.

items.label: Approval
items.detail: Signed off by someone with the right delegated authority for that value.

items.label: Sourcing
items.detail: Use a contract, quotations or a tender, depending on value and risk.

items.label: Purchase order
items.detail: Issued before delivery: item, price, quantity, delivery date, terms.

items.label: Receipt and match
items.detail: Goods received note, then invoice checked against PO and GRN.

items.label: Payment and review
items.detail: Pay on terms, record, and feed supplier performance into the next cycle.

cards.title: Put the filler-valve purchase in order
cards.prompt: Arrange the steps of a compliant purchase of spare valves for the Sheikhupura plant, from first to last.
steps: Tariq's team confirms no usable valves are in stock and raises a requisition
The requisition is approved by a manager with authority for its value
Bilal obtains competitive quotations against a written specification
A purchase order is issued to the selected supplier
Stores inspects the valves and records a goods received note
Accounts matches the invoice to the purchase order and the goods received note
The supplier is paid on the agreed terms and the file is closed

cards.title: The controls that keep P2P honest
cards.body:
- **Three-way match:** pay only when the **purchase order**, the **goods received note** and the **invoice** agree on item, quantity and price (within a small, pre-set tolerance). Services use a service-entry or completion certificate in place of the GRN.
- **Delegation of authority:** a written matrix says who may approve what value. Higher values need more senior approval, and splitting one need into several orders to stay under a limit defeats it.
- **Segregation of duties:** the person who orders should not also receive the goods, approve the invoice or change supplier bank details. Splitting these roles makes fraud need collusion.
- **PO before invoice:** an order raised after the invoice arrives (an after-the-fact PO) is a red flag; the commitment was made outside the system.
- **Maverick spend:** buying outside agreed contracts, suppliers or process. It loses negotiated prices, hides commitments and weakens control.

cards.question: An invoice for 500 cartons at PKR 90 arrives. The purchase order says 500 cartons at PKR 90, but the goods received note records 460 cartons. What should accounts do?
options: Pay the full invoice, because the PO and the invoice agree
Pay for the 460 cartons received and hold the rest until the gap is resolved
Reject the whole invoice and cancel the purchase order
Ask the supplier to issue a new PO for 460 cartons
cards.explanation: The three-way match fails on quantity, so you pay only for what the GRN confirms (460 x PKR 90 = PKR 41,400) and hold the balance until the shortage is delivered or credited. Agreement between PO and invoice alone proves nothing about delivery, and suppliers do not issue POs.

cards.title: Maverick or compliant?
cards.prompt: Zainab pulls ten transactions from last quarter. Sort each one.

items.text: Marketing books a Karachi event hotel directly, although a negotiated hotel contract exists
Stores calls off detergent from the annual rate contract with a PO
A PO is raised after the generator repair invoice has already arrived
IT buys laptops through the approved catalogue on the procurement system
A depot manager pays a local mechanic cash and claims it through expenses every week
A one-off courier charge is paid from petty cash within the petty cash limit
The plant orders lubricants from a cousin's shop, not the contracted distributor
Three quotations are taken for a PKR 400,000 printer order, as the policy requires

cards.title: The valve that only one brand can be
cards.setting: Video call with the Sheikhupura plant office. 11:30 am.

lines.text: I don't have time for tenders. Write the brand name and model number on the requisition. That brand has never failed me.
If the spec says one brand, only that brand's agent can quote. He knows it, and he will price accordingly.
Tariq, what do the valves actually have to do? Flow rate, pressure, temperature, hygiene standard, fit with the filler?
Food-grade stainless, handle 140 degree steam cleaning, fit our DN50 lines, and not leak for at least two years.
That is a specification. Write that down and three suppliers can compete. Write a brand and we have chosen the winner before we start.

cards.title: Two ways to specify
cards.caption: Most good specifications state the required performance and add design detail only where it truly matters, such as safety or fit.

items.label: Describes
items.left: What the item must achieve: output, results, standards
items.right: Exactly how it must be made: materials, dimensions, drawings

items.label: Innovation
items.left: Suppliers can offer new or cheaper solutions
items.right: Little room; suppliers build to the drawing

items.label: Risk of failure
items.left: Mainly on the supplier to meet the outcome
items.right: Mainly on the buyer, who chose the design

items.label: Competition
items.left: Usually wider
items.right: Narrower, and narrowest with a brand name

items.label: Best for
items.left: Services, equipment, solutions
items.right: Spares that must fit, safety-critical parts

cards.title: Writing a spec suppliers can compete on
cards.body:
- **Challenge the need first:** can existing stock, a repair or another site's idle asset meet it?
- State **measurable requirements** (capacity, tolerance, standard, life) instead of adjectives like 'high quality'.
- Avoid brand names. If one is unavoidable as a reference, add **'or equivalent'** and say how equivalence will be judged.
- Do not **over-specify**: every 'nice to have' written as a must narrows the field and raises the price.
- Involve the user, but let procurement check the wording for hidden bias.
- Separate **mandatory** requirements from desirable ones so evaluation is easy later.

cards.title: Tariq's brand-name requisition
cards.situation: Tariq's requisition for 24 filler valves names one Italian brand and model, with the note 'no substitutes'. The local agent for that brand has already WhatsApped Bilal a price that is 35% above last year's. Start-up is twelve weeks away and Tariq is senior and impatient. What do you do?

choices.text: Issue the PO to the agent. The plant manager knows his equipment and the timeline is tight.
choices.outcome: You get the valves, at a 35% premium, and you have taught the agent that Noor will pay whatever he asks. Auditors later ask why there was no competition and no justification for a single brand.

choices.text: Rewrite the requisition as a performance spec with Tariq (DN50 fit, 140 degree steam cleaning, food-grade stainless, two-year warranty) and invite at least three suppliers, including the agent.
choices.outcome: Tariq agrees once his real requirements are protected. Four suppliers quote, two meet the spec, and the agent drops his price by 20% once he sees competition. The decision is documented and defensible.

choices.text: Keep the brand but ask the agent for a discount because you are a big customer.
choices.outcome: The agent shaves 5% and smiles. Without a credible alternative you have no leverage, and the spec still excludes everyone else.

choices.text: Refuse the requisition until Tariq withdraws all technical requirements.
choices.outcome: Tariq escalates to the CEO, procurement looks obstructive, and the valid needs (fit, hygiene, steam cleaning) were never the problem. Challenge the brand, not the requirement.

cards.title: Spend analysis: turning a mess into a map

scenes.heading: Extract
scenes.narration: Pull every payment, invoice and purchase order for the period from accounts payable, the ERP, cards and petty cash. Spend you leave out is spend you cannot manage.

scenes.heading: Cleanse
scenes.narration: Fix the mess. One supplier may appear as three names with different spellings. Merge duplicates, correct obvious errors and convert currencies.

scenes.heading: Classify
scenes.narration: Assign each line to a category using a consistent taxonomy: packaging film, sugar, logistics, maintenance spares, IT. Vague ledger codes like 'miscellaneous' hide spend.

scenes.heading: Enrich
scenes.narration: Add useful facts: which contract applies, supplier risk ratings, whether a PO existed, payment terms.

scenes.heading: Analyse
scenes.narration: Now ask questions. Who do we spend most with? Which categories are fragmented across too many suppliers? How much spend has no contract? The answers set your priorities.

cards.title: What Noor's spend data revealed
cards.caption: Twelve months of cleansed and classified spend. The Pareto pattern is typical: a few suppliers carry most of the money.

items.label: Total third-party spend
items.detail: Across 1,140 active suppliers after merging duplicate names.

items.label: Top 60 suppliers
items.detail: PKR 3.4bn of spend sits with about 5% of the supplier base.

items.label: Packaging film
items.detail: PKR 1.3bn, almost all with one supplier: Kohsar Flexpack.

items.label: Spend with no PO
items.detail: About PKR 924m committed outside the purchase order process.

cards.question: Noor's raw data shows 'Kohsar Flexpack', 'Kohsar Flex Pack (Pvt) Ltd' and 'KOHSAR FLEXPAK' as three suppliers. Which spend analysis step fixes this?
options: Extract
Cleanse
Classify
Enrich
cards.explanation: Cleansing removes duplicates and errors, including merging one supplier recorded under several names. Classification assigns spend to categories; enrichment adds extra facts such as contracts and risk ratings.

cards.title: The Kraljic matrix
cards.caption: Two questions place every category: how much does it affect our costs and profit, and how hard or risky is it to secure supply?

items.label: Bottleneck
items.detail: Low spend, high risk. Secure supply: buffer stock, alternatives, standardise specs.

items.label: Strategic
items.detail: High spend, high risk. Long-term partnerships, joint planning, develop a second source.

items.label: Non-critical
items.detail: Low spend, low risk. Cut transaction cost: catalogues, consolidation, automation.

items.label: Leverage
items.detail: High spend, low risk. Use buying power: tenders, e-auctions, volume consolidation.

cards.title: Place Noor's categories
cards.prompt: Match each Noor Valley Foods category to its Kraljic quadrant.

pairs.right: Aseptic packaging film: 31% of spend, only two qualified makers in the region, a stop halts the plant
Refined sugar: large spend, many mills and traders, a standard commodity
A special starter culture: small spend, one approved foreign source, long lead time
Office stationery and cleaning supplies: small spend, dozens of suppliers

cards.back: Use your buying power. Consolidate volume, run competitive tenders or e-auctions, and switch suppliers if needed. Risk is low, so price pressure is safe.
Build a long-term relationship with joint planning and performance reviews, while quietly qualifying an alternative so you are never captive.
Protect supply first: safety stock, longer contracts, qualifying alternatives, or redesigning the spec so more suppliers can meet it.
Reduce the cost of buying: catalogues, framework agreements, purchasing cards, fewer suppliers, automated ordering.

In most spend data a small share of suppliers or categories (often around 20%) carries most of the value (often around 80%). Focus effort there first; the many small suppliers left (the long tail) are often worth consolidating.
No. A new supplier entering the market can turn a bottleneck into non-critical; a supplier merger can turn leverage into strategic. Review the matrix regularly.

cards.title: From analysis to a plan
cards.body:
Farah's team turns the numbers into priorities:

| Finding | Quadrant | First action |
|---|---|---|
| Film: PKR 1.3bn, one supplier | Strategic | Contract review, qualify a second source |
| Sugar: PKR 610m, 14 traders | Leverage | Consolidate to 3, tender quarterly |
| Starter culture: PKR 18m, one source | Bottleneck | Raise safety stock to 10 weeks |
| Stationery: PKR 9m, 63 suppliers | Non-critical | One catalogue supplier |

The sums check out: film is 1.3 / 4.2 = **31%** of spend. Stationery is only PKR 9m, but processing 63 suppliers' invoices costs real time, so the goal there is cheaper buying, not a hard negotiation.

Farah's rule: **spend effort where value and risk are**, and automate the rest.

cards.title: The phone call
cards.setting: Procurement floor, 5:40 pm. Bilal's phone is on speaker.

lines.text: Bilal bhai, Imran here. Resin prices are up, the rupee is down. From next month the film price rises 18%. I'm sorry, my hands are tied.
Eighteen percent? Imran sahib, we are opening a new plant on your film.
Which is why you need a reliable partner. Who else will deliver to Sheikhupura in 48 hours?
That would add over PKR 200 million a year. The plant's business case does not survive that.
Strategic category, one supplier, and he knows it. Good. Now we know where the real fight is. Stage two: we learn to source properly.

cards.title: Paper Maze cleared
items: Procure-to-pay runs need, requisition, approval, sourcing, PO, receipt, invoice match, payment, and loops back through performance data.
Pay only on a three-way match of PO, GRN and invoice; separate ordering, receiving and paying; approve within delegated limits.
After-the-fact POs and buying outside contracts are maverick spend: lost prices, hidden commitments, weak control.
Challenge the need, specify performance, avoid brand names (or add 'or equivalent'), and do not over-specify.
Spend analysis runs extract, cleanse, classify, enrich, analyse; a few suppliers usually carry most of the spend.
Kraljic: leverage (use power), strategic (partner and de-risk), bottleneck (secure supply), non-critical (cut buying cost).

cards.prompt: Think of your organisation's biggest spend category. Which Kraljic quadrant is it in, and is your current approach to it the one the matrix suggests? What is one control gap in your own procure-to-pay process?

quiz.question: Which three documents are compared in a standard three-way match before a supplier invoice for goods is paid?
options: Purchase requisition, quotation and invoice
Purchase order, goods received note and invoice
Contract, delivery challan and payment voucher
Budget approval, purchase order and bank statement
quiz.explanation: The three-way match compares what was ordered (purchase order), what was received (goods received note) and what is being billed (invoice). A requisition and quotation come earlier in the cycle and do not prove delivery.

quiz.question: Noor's marketing team books a large event at a Karachi hotel directly, even though procurement has a negotiated corporate rate contract with another hotel. What is this best described as?
options: A bottleneck purchase
Segregation of duties
Maverick spend
A performance specification
quiz.explanation: Buying outside agreed contracts or process is maverick spend: the negotiated rate is lost and the commitment bypasses procurement controls. It has nothing to do with Kraljic quadrants or specification type.

quiz.question: In a compliant procure-to-pay cycle, what should happen immediately before stores records a goods received note?
options: The supplier is paid in full for the order on agreed terms
Accounts matches the invoice against the order and receipt
The user raises a purchase requisition for approval
The PO is issued and the goods are delivered
quiz.explanation: The PO is issued, the supplier delivers, and stores then inspects and records the receipt. Invoice matching and payment come after receipt; the requisition comes much earlier.

quiz.question: Bilal needs a cleaning service for the new plant. He writes: 'All production floors to pass the weekly hygiene swab test; zero pest sightings; response to spills within 30 minutes.' What type of specification is this?
options: A performance (functional) specification
A technical (design) specification
A brand-name specification
A conformance-only specification with fixed methods
quiz.explanation: It states outcomes the supplier must achieve, not the methods, chemicals or staffing to use. That is a performance specification, which leaves suppliers free to propose how they will meet the results.

quiz.question: Why should a specification normally avoid naming a single brand?
options: Because brand-name goods are always lower quality than generic equivalents on the market
It restricts competition, often to one agent, weakening the buyer's price position
Because suppliers are not legally allowed to sell branded goods to companies in Pakistan
Because brand names make the three-way match of PO, GRN and invoice impossible to complete
quiz.explanation: A brand name effectively chooses the winner before sourcing starts, so only that brand's agent can respond and price pressure disappears. If a brand reference is unavoidable, add 'or equivalent' and define how equivalence is judged.

quiz.question: During spend analysis, Zainab finds PKR 140 million booked to 'Miscellaneous expenses'. Which step should break this down so it can be managed?
options: Extract
Enrich with contract data
Classify
Payment
quiz.explanation: Classification assigns each spend line to a category in a consistent taxonomy. 'Miscellaneous' is exactly the kind of vague code that hides manageable spend. Enrichment adds facts such as contract status once lines are classified.

quiz.question: Refined sugar is a large share of Noor's spend and is available from many mills and traders. Where does it sit on the Kraljic matrix?
options: Leverage
Strategic
Bottleneck
Non-critical
quiz.explanation: High profit impact with low supply risk is the leverage quadrant. Strategic items are high on both axes; bottleneck items are low impact but high risk.

quiz.question: A low-value laboratory reagent used in quality testing has only one approved source abroad and a 14-week lead time. Which approach best fits its Kraljic quadrant?
options: Run an e-auction to cut the price
Buy it through a purchasing card to cut transaction cost
Treat the supplier as a strategic partner with joint product development
Secure supply with safety stock and work to qualify an alternative
quiz.explanation: Low spend with high supply risk is a bottleneck item. The priority is continuity of supply: buffer stock, longer agreements and alternatives. An e-auction suits leverage items and is pointless with one source.

quiz.question: Noor spends PKR 4.2 billion a year, of which PKR 3.4 billion goes to its top 60 suppliers out of 1,140. Roughly what share of spend do the top 60 carry?
options: About 5%
About 81%
About 60%
Nearly all, about 95%
quiz.explanation: 3.4 / 4.2 = 0.81, so about 81% of spend sits with the top 60 suppliers. Those 60 are about 5% of the supplier base (60 / 1,140), which is the Pareto pattern that tells you where to focus.

quiz.question: At a depot, the same storekeeper raises purchase orders, signs the goods received notes and updates supplier bank details. What is the main control weakness?
options: Lack of a performance specification for the items the depot buys regularly
Too many suppliers in a non-critical category, raising the cost of each transaction
No segregation of duties: one person could create and pay a fake purchase
The delegation of authority is too strict for a busy depot to work with
quiz.explanation: When one person can order, confirm receipt and change where money is paid, a fraudulent order can be created and paid without anyone else's involvement. Splitting these duties means fraud needs collusion.

sessions.title: Sourcing Strategy and Tendering
sessions.summary: Choose how many suppliers to use and how to approach the market, then run a fair tender: RFI, RFQ or RFP, single or two-stage, one or two envelopes, mandatory and weighted criteria, and a weighted scoring calculation you can defend.
objectives: Compare sole, single, dual and multiple sourcing and choose a sourcing route for a category
Choose between an RFI, RFQ and RFP and between single-stage and two-stage, one- and two-envelope methods
Design evaluation criteria with mandatory pass/fail tests, weights fixed in advance and a clear scoring scale
Calculate price scores and weighted totals, and handle clarifications, abnormally low bids and conflicts properly

cards.title: Three tenders, ten weeks
cards.setting: Procurement war room, Gulberg. A printed plant layout covers the table.

lines.text: Ten weeks left. Three sourcing jobs: cartons for the plant, a third-party logistics partner to run the Sheikhupura warehouse, and the effluent treatment plant.
Cartons are easy: standard spec, lots of converters. The 3PL is a service, every bidder will propose something different. The effluent plant... honestly, we don't know yet what the best design is.
For logistics, just give it to Shah sahib's company. They moved my old plant for years. I trust them.
Trust is nice. Finance needs a decision we can defend to the board and the auditors.
Then Shah sahib can bid like everyone else. Three different buys need three different routes. Let's choose them properly.

scenes.heading: Do you know the market?
scenes.narration: If you don't yet know who can supply or what solutions exist, start with a request for information. It asks suppliers about themselves and their capabilities, without asking for a binding price.

scenes.heading: Is the need fully specified?
scenes.narration: When you can describe exactly what you want, such as a standard carton, send a request for quotation. Suppliers compete mainly on price and delivery against the same spec.

scenes.heading: Is it a solution?
scenes.narration: When suppliers will propose different ways to meet your need, as with a logistics service, send a request for proposal. You judge quality and price together, using weighted criteria.

scenes.heading: Can you write the spec yet?
scenes.narration: If the technical answer is still unclear, use two stages. First, take technical proposals without prices and discuss them. Then fix the spec and ask everyone for final technical and priced bids.

scenes.heading: Keep price from colouring quality
scenes.narration: With two envelopes, technical and financial bids are sealed separately. The technical envelopes are scored first; only bidders who pass have their prices opened.

cards.title: From market to contract
cards.caption: Each step narrows the field fairly, using criteria set before suppliers respond.

items.label: Market scan and RFI
items.detail: Learn who is out there and what they can do.

items.label: Prequalification
items.detail: Shortlist on capacity, finances, certifications and experience.

items.label: RFQ or RFP issued
items.detail: Same documents, criteria and deadline to every shortlisted bidder.

items.label: Responsive bids
items.detail: Bids that meet every mandatory requirement go forward.

items.label: Evaluation and award
items.detail: Weighted scoring, approval, award and debrief.

cards.back: Only one supplier in the market can provide the item, for example because of a patent. You have no choice, so manage the risk.
Other suppliers exist, but you choose to buy from one, for simplicity or a better price. It is a decision you can revisit.
Two suppliers share the volume, often 70/30, so each stays sharp and one can cover if the other fails.
Several suppliers share a commodity need. It maximises competition but can raise admin cost and weaken each relationship.
Screening suppliers on capability before inviting full bids, so only those able to deliver spend effort bidding.
A formal round in which every shortlisted bidder may improve its offer once, under the same rules and deadline. Used in private-sector tenders where policy allows.

cards.title: Which document?
cards.prompt: Match each of Noor's needs to the best opening move.

pairs.right: Finding out which firms in Pakistan can recycle used aseptic cartons, and how
Buying 2 million corrugated cartons to a fixed drawing and board grade
Appointing a 3PL partner to design and run the Sheikhupura warehouse operation
An effluent treatment plant where the best technology is not yet clear
Ordering more stretch wrap under an existing annual rate contract

cards.question: Noor wants a payroll outsourcing service and expects bidders to propose different software, staffing and service models. Which request fits best?
options: Request for quotation
Request for proposal
Request for information only
Direct purchase order
cards.explanation: When suppliers will offer different solutions and you must judge quality and price together, an RFP with weighted criteria fits. An RFQ suits a fully specified need compared mainly on price. An RFI gathers market information but does not lead directly to a contract.

items.label: When
items.left: Spec is complete and clear
items.right: Spec cannot be fully written yet; complex or technical

items.label: Stage one
items.left: Full technical and priced bids, once
items.right: Technical proposals without price, then discussions

items.label: Stage two
items.left: None
items.right: Revised spec; all bidders submit final technical and priced bids

items.label: Strength
items.left: Fast and simple
items.right: Lets the buyer learn before fixing the spec

items.label: Watch out
items.left: A poor spec gives poor bids
items.right: Takes longer; keep discussions equal for all bidders

cards.title: One envelope or two?
cards.body:
**One envelope:** technical and price are submitted together and opened together. Simple and fine for standard goods, but evaluators see prices while scoring quality.

**Two envelopes:** the technical proposal and the financial proposal are sealed **separately** and handed in at the same time.

1. Technical envelopes are opened and evaluated first.
2. Bidders who fail the technical stage have their financial envelopes **returned unopened**.
3. Financial envelopes of technically qualified bidders are opened, ideally in the presence of bidders who wish to attend.
4. Price and technical results are combined (or the lowest-priced qualified bid wins, if the documents say so).

Methods combine: **single-stage one-envelope**, **single-stage two-envelope**, **two-stage** and **two-stage two-envelope**. The point of two envelopes is that **price cannot colour the quality score**.

cards.title: Open the 3PL envelopes
cards.prompt: Bilal runs a single-stage two-envelope RFP for the 3PL contract. Put the steps in order.
steps: Bidders submit sealed technical and financial envelopes by the deadline
Technical envelopes are opened and recorded; financial envelopes stay sealed
The committee scores technical proposals against the published criteria
Qualified bidders' financial envelopes are opened; failed bidders' envelopes are returned unopened
Technical and price scores are combined to rank the bidders
The award is approved and unsuccessful bidders are offered a debrief

cards.title: The cheapest bid that wasn't
cards.setting: Evaluation committee room. Three thick 3PL proposals on the table.

lines.text: Shah sahib's company didn't submit the mandatory food-safety certificate for its warehouse. The RFP said: no certificate, no further evaluation.
It's paperwork. They're applying for it. Let them send it next week.
If we accept a missing mandatory document from one bidder, we have changed the rules after seeing the bids. The others could have bid differently too.
And of the three compliant bids, the cheapest isn't automatically the best. We set weights: price 40, technical 30, experience 20, sustainability 10.
Score them independently first, then we moderate. Show me the numbers.

cards.title: Building defensible evaluation criteria
cards.caption: Criteria, weights and the scoring method are fixed before bids arrive and published in the tender documents.

items.label: Mandatory pass/fail
items.detail: Licences, certifications, bid security, key spec items. Fail one and the bid is non-responsive.

items.label: Weighted criteria
items.detail: Price, technical, experience, sustainability: weights add to 100%.

items.label: Scoring scale
items.detail: Define what 0, 5 and 10 look like for each criterion so evaluators score alike.

items.label: Price formula
items.detail: Common method: lowest price divided by bid price, times the maximum score.

items.label: Score and moderate
items.detail: Evaluators score alone, then agree a moderated score and record reasons.

cards.title: Scoring the three compliant 3PL bids
cards.body:
Weights: **price 40%, technical 30%, experience 20%, sustainability 10%**. Scores out of 10. Price score = lowest price / bid price x 10.

| | A | B | C |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3-year price (PKR m) | 96 | 120 | 108 |
| Price score | 10.00 | 8.00 | 8.89 |
| Technical | 6 | 9 | 8 |
| Experience | 7 | 8 | 6 |
| Sustainability | 5 | 8 | 7 |

Weighted totals (score x weight, summed):

- **A:** 4.00 + 1.80 + 1.40 + 0.50 = **7.70**
- **B:** 3.20 + 2.70 + 1.60 + 0.80 = **8.30**
- **C:** 3.56 + 2.40 + 1.20 + 0.70 = **7.86**

B wins, despite the highest price, because the published weights value its stronger solution. Had the weights been chosen after seeing the bids, nobody could trust this result.

cards.title: 3PL tender result
cards.caption: Weighted totals out of 10, using the weights published in the RFP.

items.label: Bidder B
items.detail: Highest price, strongest technical and sustainability scores. Recommended.

items.label: Bidder C
items.detail: Middle price, good technical plan, thinner experience.

items.label: Bidder A
items.detail: Lowest price, weakest technical solution.

items.label: Shah sahib's firm
items.detail: Missing mandatory food-safety certificate; not scored.

cards.question: In an RFQ, the lowest compliant price is PKR 1.8 million. Using 'lowest price / bid price x 10', what price score does a bid of PKR 2.4 million get?
cards.explanation: 1.8 / 2.4 = 0.75, and 0.75 x 10 = 7.5. The lowest bid gets the full 10; others score in proportion to how close they are to it.

cards.title: The WhatsApp discount
cards.situation: Two days after the financial envelopes are opened, Bidder A's director messages Bilal on WhatsApp: 'We can drop our price 15% if that helps. Just tell me the number to beat.' That would make A's price PKR 81.6m and might change the ranking. Tariq says, 'Great, take it, it saves money.' What do you advise?

choices.text: Accept the new price and re-score A. Savings are savings.
choices.outcome: A now ranks first, B and C learn that one bidder got a private second chance, and B files a complaint. The process is no longer fair and the award is hard to defend.

choices.text: Decline, record the approach, and evaluate the bids as submitted. If the documents allowed a BAFO, any improvement must be invited from all shortlisted bidders equally.
choices.outcome: Fairness is kept. B's award stands on the published rules, and the file shows the unsolicited approach was refused. Bidders learn Noor's tenders cannot be gamed.

choices.text: Tell A the number to beat so the competition is sharper.
choices.outcome: You have leaked a rival's confidential price. That is a serious integrity breach, and it exposes Noor to complaints and reputational damage.

choices.text: Ignore the message but say nothing to anyone.
choices.outcome: You did not take the bait, which is good, but an unrecorded approach leaves no trail if questions arise later. Record and report it.

cards.title: Clarification or change of bid?
cards.prompt: During evaluation the committee may ask bidders to clarify, but not to change the substance of their bids. Sort each request.

items.text: Asking a bidder to confirm which warehouse address its proposal refers to
Letting a bidder reduce its price after prices were opened
Asking for a missing page reference in an otherwise complete method statement
Allowing a bidder to add a mandatory certificate it failed to submit
Asking a bidder to explain how its unusually low labour cost was calculated
Letting a bidder swap its proposed site manager for a stronger one
Asking a bidder to confirm an obvious arithmetic total in its price schedule
Accepting an alternative design submitted after the deadline

cards.title: Evaluation traps to avoid
cards.body:
- **Abnormally low bids:** do not just celebrate. Ask the bidder to explain its costs. A price that cannot cover wages, materials or taxes often leads to failure or claims later.
- **Moving goalposts:** never add, drop or reweight criteria after bids are opened.
- **Conflicts:** every evaluator signs a declaration of interest. A member with a link to a bidder steps aside from that tender.
- **Group think:** evaluators score independently first, then moderate and record the reasons for the agreed score.
- **Debrief:** offer unsuccessful bidders feedback on their own scores. It builds trust and better bids next time.

cards.title: A new kind of tender
cards.setting: Farah's office, 6:15 pm. Board pack on the desk.

lines.text: Board approved Bidder B for the 3PL. They liked that we could show every score. One more thing: the board wants us to bid for a government school-milk programme.
So this time Noor is the supplier, in a public tender. Different rules, I think. No WhatsApp discounts there either.
And I still want proper chillers for the plant, not the cheapest ones. The cheap ones eat electricity.
Two lessons for stage three, then: how public procurement works in Pakistan, and how to compare the whole cost of owning something, not just its price.

cards.title: Tender Hall cleared
items: Sole source means no alternative exists; single source is a choice. Dual sourcing keeps a backup and competitive tension.
RFI to learn the market, RFQ for a fully specified need, RFP when suppliers propose solutions judged on quality and price.
Two-stage tenders let you refine an unclear spec before prices; two envelopes stop price colouring the technical score.
Fix mandatory criteria, weights, scoring scale and price formula before bids arrive, and publish them.
Price score = lowest price / bid price x maximum; weighted total = sum of score x weight. The cheapest bid need not win.
Clarify, never let bidders change substance after opening; probe abnormally low bids; declare conflicts; debrief losers.

cards.prompt: Recall the last tender or quotation exercise you took part in. Were the criteria and weights fixed and shared before bids arrived, and would the result have survived a complaint from a losing bidder?

quiz.question: Noor wants to learn which Pakistani firms can recycle used aseptic cartons and what methods they use, before deciding whether to run a tender. Which document fits?
options: Request for information (RFI)
Request for quotation (RFQ)
Purchase order to a likely supplier
Best and final offer
quiz.explanation: An RFI gathers market information about suppliers and their capabilities without asking for binding prices. An RFQ assumes you already know exactly what you want; a BAFO comes at the end of a competitive process.

quiz.question: Bilal is buying 2 million corrugated cartons to a fixed drawing, board grade and print. Several converters can make them. Which route is most efficient?
options: Request for information followed by a two-stage tender
Request for proposal with heavily weighted technical criteria
Request for quotation against the fixed specification
Direct award to the plant manager's preferred converter
quiz.explanation: With a complete specification and many capable suppliers, an RFQ lets suppliers compete on price and delivery against the same requirement. Two-stage tenders and RFPs are for needs where the solution is still open.

quiz.question: Several mills can supply Noor's sugar, but Noor buys it all from one mill because of a good price and simple logistics. What is this arrangement called?
options: Sole sourcing
Dual sourcing
Multiple sourcing
Single sourcing
quiz.explanation: Single sourcing is choosing one supplier when alternatives exist. Sole sourcing means no alternative exists in the market. Dual and multiple sourcing split the volume among two or more suppliers.

quiz.question: In an RFQ the lowest compliant price is PKR 800,000. Using the formula 'lowest price / bid price x 10', what price score does a bid of PKR 1,000,000 receive?
quiz.explanation: 800,000 / 1,000,000 = 0.8, and 0.8 x 10 = 8. The lowest bid scores 10; a bid 25% higher scores 8, not 7.5, because the formula divides the lowest price by the bid.

quiz.question: Weights are price 50%, quality 30% and delivery 20%. A bid scores price 8, quality 6 and delivery 10 (all out of 10). What is its weighted total out of 10?
quiz.explanation: 8 x 0.5 = 4.0; 6 x 0.3 = 1.8; 10 x 0.2 = 2.0. Total 4.0 + 1.8 + 2.0 = 7.8. A simple average of the three scores (8.0) ignores the weights.

quiz.question: In a two-envelope tender, what normally happens to the financial envelope of a bidder whose technical proposal fails?
options: It is returned to the bidder unopened
It is opened, but the price is given a 10% penalty
It is opened first so the committee can see if the bid is worth rescuing
It is kept sealed and used as the reference price for negotiation
quiz.explanation: The point of two envelopes is that price never influences the technical assessment. Prices of technically non-responsive bidders are not opened; their envelopes are returned unopened.

quiz.question: Noor needs an effluent treatment plant. The engineers are unsure which treatment technology is best for its waste stream. Which tendering method best fits?
options: A single-stage one-envelope RFQ, judged on the lowest price for a standard design
A reverse e-auction on price among every firm that has built a treatment plant in Pakistan
A two-stage tender: technical proposals and discussions, then priced bids to a refined spec
A call-off from an existing stationery framework
quiz.explanation: Two-stage tendering is designed for complex needs where the spec cannot be fully written at the start. Stage one lets the buyer learn from technical proposals; stage two gets comparable priced bids against the refined requirement.

quiz.question: When should evaluation criteria and their weights for an RFP be decided and shared with bidders?
options: After the technical envelopes are opened, so weights can match what bidders offered
Before bids are submitted, in the tender documents
After the financial envelopes are opened
Only at the debrief, so bidders cannot game the criteria
quiz.explanation: Criteria, weights and the scoring method must be fixed and published before bids arrive. Setting or changing them after seeing bids allows the outcome to be steered and makes the award indefensible.

quiz.question: An RFP states that a valid food-safety certificate is mandatory. The lowest-priced bidder did not include one and offers to send it next week. What should the committee do?
options: Treat the bid as non-responsive and not evaluate it further
Accept the certificate next week, since the bid is cheapest
Score the bid normally but deduct points for the missing certificate
Extend the deadline for this bidder only
quiz.explanation: Mandatory requirements are pass/fail. Accepting a missing mandatory document from one bidder after the deadline changes the rules for that bidder alone and is unfair to those who complied. Scoring it as a deduction turns a pass/fail test into a weighted one.

quiz.question: During evaluation, which of these is an acceptable clarification request to a bidder?
options: Inviting the bidder to lower its price so that it matches a cheaper rival's offer
Allowing the bidder to replace its proposed project manager
Allowing the bidder to submit a missing mandatory licence
Asking the bidder to explain how it calculated an unusually low labour cost
quiz.explanation: A clarification helps the committee understand the bid as submitted, including probing an abnormally low price. Changing price, staff or adding missing mandatory documents alters the substance of the bid after the deadline.

sessions.title: Public Procurement in Pakistan and Total Cost of Ownership
sessions.summary: See procurement from the other side of the table: how Pakistan's public procurement framework works, how it differs from private practice, and how a supplier should behave in a public tender. Then learn to compare options on total cost of ownership, not price tag.
objectives: Describe Pakistan's federal and provincial public procurement framework and its core principles in general terms
Contrast public procurement rules with private-sector practice, including negotiation, publication and complaints
Behave correctly as a bidder in a public tender, using formal channels only
Calculate total cost of ownership, landed cost and simple payback to compare options

cards.title: The school-milk tender
cards.setting: Conference room, Noor Valley Foods. The tender notice is on the screen.

lines.text: A provincial education department is tendering for flavoured milk for government schools. Open competitive bidding, bids due in four weeks.
Easy. My college friend is a deputy secretary there. One phone call and we'll know what they really want.
Tariq, that phone call could get us disqualified, or worse. In a public tender, every bidder gets the same information through the same channel.
And the bidding documents already say how they will evaluate: lowest evaluated responsive bid, with mandatory food-safety and capacity criteria.
Stage three: the Public Gate. We learn the rules that govern government buying, and we play by them.

cards.title: How public buying works in Pakistan

scenes.heading: Public money, public rules
scenes.narration: When a government body buys, it spends taxpayers' money. So the law sets rules for how it must buy, not just internal policy.

scenes.heading: Federal and provincial
scenes.narration: At federal level, the Public Procurement Regulatory Authority, created by an ordinance in 2002, oversees rules made in 2004. Each province has its own procurement law and authority. Which rules apply depends on who is buying.

scenes.heading: Open by default
scenes.narration: Open competitive bidding is the normal method. Tenders are advertised publicly, documents state the evaluation criteria, and bids are opened in public at a stated time.

scenes.heading: Limited exceptions
scenes.narration: Other methods, such as quotations for small purchases or direct contracting, are allowed only in defined situations and within set limits, and the reason must be recorded. Splitting a known need into small orders to fit a lighter method is not allowed.

scenes.heading: Checks and complaints
scenes.narration: Results are made public before the contract is signed, bidders can complain to a grievance committee, and firms found in corrupt practice can be blacklisted.

cards.title: Public versus private procurement
cards.caption: Good private practice borrows a lot from public rules, but the private sector has more freedom.

items.label: Governed by
items.left: Procurement law and rules, federal or provincial
items.right: Company policy, contract law, board approvals

items.label: Default method
items.left: Open competitive bidding, advertised
items.right: Whatever policy allows: invited bids, RFQs, direct deals

items.label: Negotiation after bids
items.left: Generally not permitted
items.right: Allowed: BAFO or negotiation within policy

items.label: Transparency
items.left: Criteria, openings and results made public
items.right: Usually confidential

items.label: Complaints
items.left: Formal grievance mechanism
items.right: Commercial discussion or courts

cards.title: A typical public tender, step by step

items.label: Plan
items.detail: The agency includes the need in its annual procurement plan and budget.

items.label: Advertise
items.detail: Notice published as the rules require, with a minimum time to respond.

items.label: Bidding documents
items.detail: Spec, criteria, bid security, contract terms; written pre-bid queries answered to all.

items.label: Public opening
items.detail: Bids opened at the stated time, in front of bidders who attend.

items.label: Evaluate and publish
items.detail: Only the published criteria are used; the evaluation result is made public before award.

items.label: Award and contract
items.detail: After any complaints are handled; winner gives a performance guarantee.

cards.title: Always check the current rules
cards.body:
Public procurement rules change through amendments, regulations and new systems. Thresholds for each method, advertising timelines, bid security limits and the use of the national e-procurement system (**e-PADS**) have all been revised over time, and provinces differ.

- First confirm **which framework** applies: federal, or a specific province.
- Read the **bidding documents** carefully; they apply the rules to that tender.
- Check the **regulator's website** for the latest rules and amendments before quoting any figure.
- In this course, figures are described generally on purpose. Do not rely on memory or on old training slides.

cards.back: The default public method: openly advertised, any eligible firm may bid, criteria stated in advance.
A guarantee (often a bank guarantee or pay order) submitted with the bid, forfeited if the bidder withdraws improperly or refuses to sign. Its maximum is capped by the rules.
Security given by the winning bidder when signing the contract, to protect the buyer if the contract is not performed.
A committee in the procuring agency that hears bidders' complaints about the process before or after evaluation.
Barring a firm from bidding for a period after corrupt or fraudulent practice or serious non-performance.
A signed undertaking by bidders, usually for larger contracts, that they have not paid and will not pay bribes or commissions to win.
Pakistan's national electronic procurement system, through which agencies increasingly must advertise, receive and evaluate bids. Check which agencies it now covers.

cards.question: After a federal public tender's bids are opened, the lowest evaluated bidder offers the agency a further 5% discount if it signs this week. What is the general position?
options: The agency should accept, as it improves value for money
Negotiation with bidders after opening is generally not permitted in public procurement
The agency must invite all bidders to a reverse auction
The discount may be accepted if the bidder confirms it in writing
cards.explanation: Public procurement rules generally prohibit negotiating with bidders after opening, because it would let one bidder improve its position outside the open process. Private buyers have more freedom, for example a BAFO round if their policy and documents allow it.

cards.title: Public, private or both?
cards.prompt: Sort each practice: normal in private practice but generally not allowed in public tenders, or expected in both?

items.text: Negotiating price with the top-ranked bidder after bids are opened
Fixing evaluation criteria before bids are received
Inviting only three known suppliers without any advertisement, for a large contract
Declaring and managing conflicts of interest among evaluators
Keeping the evaluation result confidential from losing bidders
Treating every bidder equally on information and deadlines
Directly awarding a large contract because the supplier is trusted
Keeping a written record of why the winner was chosen

cards.title: Tariq's friendly call
cards.situation: Bids for the school-milk tender are due in ten days. Bilal has two questions about the pack size and delivery schedule in the bidding documents. Tariq says: 'Don't waste time on formal letters. I'll call my friend, the deputy secretary, tonight and ask what they really want, and whether our price is in the right range.' What do you advise?

choices.text: Let Tariq call; it's just a question, and everyone uses contacts.
choices.outcome: If it comes out, Noor could be disqualified and face blacklisting, and the official could face disciplinary action. Even an innocent call looks like seeking an unfair advantage.

choices.text: Send the questions in writing through the channel and before the deadline stated in the bidding documents, and make sure nobody contacts officials informally.
choices.outcome: The agency answers in writing and shares the answer with all bidders. Noor bids on the same information as everyone else, and nobody can question how it won or lost.

choices.text: Skip the questions and price high to cover all possibilities.
choices.outcome: You stay clean, which is good, but you may lose the tender on price or misread a requirement. Clarification through the proper channel is there to be used.

choices.text: Ask a junior employee with no family link to call the department instead.
choices.outcome: Changing who calls does not change what the call is. Informal contact to gain information is still improper.

cards.question: Noor, as a bidder, has a question about the delivery schedule in a public tender. How should the agency's answer normally be handled?
options: Given only to Noor, since Noor asked
Given by phone to keep it quick
Given in writing and shared with all bidders who obtained the documents
Withheld until after bids are opened
cards.explanation: Pre-bid clarifications are answered in writing and circulated to everyone holding the bidding documents (without naming who asked), so all bidders compete on the same information.

cards.title: Two chillers, one argument
cards.setting: Plant office, Sheikhupura. Two quotations pinned to the board.

lines.text: Chiller A is PKR 4.0 million. Chiller B is PKR 5.2 million. Same capacity. The budget is tight. A is the obvious choice.
A uses a lot more electricity. We run 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. It will cost us more every single month.
B's maintenance contract is cheaper too, and its resale value after five years is higher.
Then stop comparing price tags. Put every cost of owning each chiller for five years on one page. The total decides.

cards.title: The TCO iceberg
cards.caption: The purchase price is only the visible tip. Most of the cost of owning equipment sits below the waterline.

items.label: Purchase price
items.detail: The quoted price: what most people compare.

items.label: Acquisition costs
items.detail: Freight, duties, installation, commissioning, training.

items.label: Operating costs
items.detail: Energy, consumables, operators, insurance.

items.label: Maintenance and downtime
items.detail: Service contracts, spares, lost production when it fails.

items.label: End of life
items.detail: Removal and disposal, minus any resale or residual value.

cards.title: Total cost of ownership, simply
cards.body:
**TCO = acquisition costs + operating costs + maintenance and downtime costs + disposal costs - residual (resale) value**, over a stated period.

- Use the **same period** for every option, normally the expected life or contract term.
- Include **downtime** where failure stops production: hours lost x cost per hour.
- For imports, compare **landed cost**: price at origin + freight and insurance + duties and taxes + clearing and inland transport + the extra cost of holding more stock.
- **Payback** for a dearer but cheaper-to-run option = extra upfront cost / yearly saving.
- For long lives or large sums, discount future costs to present value; a rupee in year five is worth less than a rupee today.

TCO thinking applies in public tenders too, but only when the bidding documents say life-cycle costs will be evaluated.

cards.title: The chiller decision in numbers
cards.body:
Five-year view, PKR millions (undiscounted):

| Cost | Chiller A | Chiller B |
|---|---|---|
| Purchase price | 4.0 | 5.2 |
| Installation | 0.3 | 0.3 |
| Energy (per year) | 1.2 | 0.9 |
| Energy x 5 years | 6.0 | 4.5 |
| Maintenance (0.3 / 0.2 per year) x 5 | 1.5 | 1.0 |
| Less resale value | -0.2 | -0.5 |
| **TCO** | **11.6** | **10.5** |

B costs **PKR 1.2m more** to buy but saves **PKR 0.4m a year** in energy and maintenance (0.3 + 0.1). **Payback = 1.2 / 0.4 = 3 years**, and over five years B is **PKR 1.1m cheaper** to own. Zainab approves B, with the calculation in the file.

items.label: TCO Chiller A
items.detail: Cheapest to buy, most expensive to own over five years.

items.label: TCO Chiller B
items.detail: Higher price, lower energy and maintenance, better resale.

items.label: Five-year saving with B
items.detail: About 9% lower total cost of ownership.

items.label: Payback on B's premium
items.detail: PKR 1.2m extra price recovered at PKR 0.4m a year.

cards.title: Where does each cost belong?
cards.prompt: Match each item from Bilal's TCO worksheet to its TCO component.

pairs.right: Customs clearing and transport of a new boiler from Karachi port to Sheikhupura
Gas consumed by the boiler every month
Lost production while the boiler waits for an imported spare part
The price a scrap dealer pays for the old boiler, less removal costs
Sending two operators to the supplier's training centre before start-up

cards.title: Running a TCO comparison
cards.prompt: Put Bilal's steps for comparing two packaging machines in order.
steps: Agree the comparison period, such as the machine's expected seven-year life
List every cost element from acquisition to disposal
Collect data for each option: quotes, energy use, maintenance terms, failure rates
Calculate each option's costs over the period and subtract residual value
Test the result against key assumptions, such as energy prices
Recommend the option with the best total value and record the calculation

cards.question: A boiler costs PKR 900,000 more than the alternative but saves PKR 300,000 a year in gas. What is the simple payback period?
options: 2 years
3 years
4 years
9 years
cards.explanation: Payback = extra upfront cost / yearly saving = 900,000 / 300,000 = 3 years. After that, the saving is pure benefit for the rest of the boiler's life.

cards.title: Public Gate cleared
items: Federal public procurement is overseen by PPRA (2002 ordinance, 2004 rules); each province has its own law and authority. Check which applies.
Open competitive bidding is the default; other methods only in defined cases with recorded reasons. Splitting to dodge rules is not allowed.
Public tenders: criteria published in advance, public bid opening, results made public before award, complaints to a grievance committee, no post-bid negotiation.
As a bidder, ask questions only in writing through the stated channel; informal contact with officials risks disqualification or blacklisting.
TCO = acquisition + operating + maintenance and downtime + disposal - residual value, over the same period for every option.
Payback = extra upfront cost / yearly saving. Landed cost adds freight, duties, clearing and extra stock to the import price.

cards.prompt: Pick an item your team bought mainly on price. If you had calculated its total cost of ownership, which hidden costs would have appeared, and would the decision have changed?

quiz.question: Which body oversees public procurement rules for federal government agencies in Pakistan?
options: The Competition Commission of Pakistan
The State Bank of Pakistan
The Public Procurement Regulatory Authority (PPRA)
Each federal ministry's own finance wing, with no central regulator
quiz.explanation: The federal PPRA, established by an ordinance in 2002, oversees the federal public procurement rules made in 2004. Provinces have their own procurement laws and authorities. The Competition Commission deals with anti-competitive conduct such as cartels.

quiz.question: What is the default (principal) method of procurement for goods, works and services under Pakistan's public procurement rules?
options: Direct contracting with a trusted supplier
Negotiated tendering
Open competitive bidding
Request for quotations from three suppliers
quiz.explanation: Open competitive bidding is the normal method. Quotations, direct contracting and other methods are allowed only in defined circumstances and limits, with the reason recorded.

quiz.question: Which practice is normal in private-sector procurement but generally NOT permitted in Pakistani public procurement?
options: Negotiating price with a bidder after bids have been opened
Stating evaluation criteria in the tender documents
Keeping a written record of the evaluation
Requiring every evaluator to declare any conflicts of interest
quiz.explanation: Public rules generally prohibit negotiation with bidders after opening. The other three are good practice expected in both sectors.

quiz.question: Noor, as a bidder in a public tender, wants to ask about the pack size in the specification. What is the correct way?
options: Call a known official in the department to get a quick answer
In writing, through the channel and by the deadline in the bidding documents
Include the question inside the sealed bid so the evaluation committee can answer it
Ask the question publicly at the bid opening ceremony
quiz.explanation: Pre-bid questions go in writing through the stated channel. The answer is shared with all bidders so everyone competes on the same information. Informal calls create an unfair advantage and risk disqualification.

quiz.question: Why are bids in a public open tender normally opened in public at a stated time?
options: To let bidders compare prices and negotiate with each other before the formal evaluation starts
So the agency can announce and confirm the winning bidder on the spot at the opening
So the evaluation committee can skip the technical evaluation
So bidders see that all bids were received and read out as submitted, reducing tampering
quiz.explanation: Public opening at the stated time, in front of bidders who attend, shows that all bids were received and recorded as submitted. Evaluation still follows afterwards against the published criteria.

quiz.question: Which of these is an operating cost in a total cost of ownership calculation for a packaging machine?
options: The electricity it uses each month
Its installation and commissioning on site
Its resale value after seven years
Its customs clearing at the port
quiz.explanation: Energy used in running the machine is an operating cost. Installation and clearing are acquisition costs, and resale value is an end-of-life item that reduces TCO.

quiz.question: Over four years, a pump costs PKR 600,000 to buy, PKR 150,000 a year to run and PKR 50,000 a year to maintain, with no resale value. What is its four-year TCO?
quiz.explanation: 600,000 + (150,000 + 50,000) x 4 = 600,000 + 800,000 = PKR 1,400,000. PKR 800,000 adds only one year of running and maintenance to the price.

quiz.question: An energy-efficient compressor costs PKR 1.5 million more than a standard one but saves PKR 500,000 a year in electricity. What is the simple payback period?
options: 1.5 years
5 years
2 years
3 years
quiz.explanation: Payback = extra cost / yearly saving = 1,500,000 / 500,000 = 3 years.

quiz.question: A bidder in a public tender believes the evaluation criteria were applied wrongly. Where should it normally take its complaint first?
options: To the procuring agency's grievance redressal committee
To the media, to put pressure on the agency
To the winning bidder, to negotiate a share of the contract
To the Competition Commission, as the first step
quiz.explanation: Public procurement rules provide a grievance mechanism within the procuring agency for complaints about the process. Other bodies may become relevant later, but the formal complaint route starts with the agency's grievance committee.

quiz.question: A government department needs PKR 9 million of printing over the year but places twelve separate monthly orders, each small enough for a simple quotation method. What is the main concern?
options: Monthly orders always cost more in freight
Splitting a known need into small orders to avoid open bidding, which the rules forbid
The department should use a two-envelope tender for each monthly order
There is no real concern, because each separate monthly order follows the quotation rules
quiz.explanation: The annual need is known, so splitting it into small orders to fit a lighter method avoids the competition the rules require. Planning should combine the need into one properly advertised procurement, perhaps with scheduled deliveries.

sessions.title: Negotiation and Contracts
sessions.summary: Face Imran's 18% price rise with evidence and a plan: BATNA, ZOPA, anchoring and traded concessions. Then lock the deal into a contract that works: key clauses, Incoterms for imports, SLAs with service credits and liquidated damages that hold up.
objectives: Prepare a negotiation with objectives, a BATNA, a walk-away point and a should-cost analysis
Identify the ZOPA, use and resist anchoring, and trade concessions rather than give them away
Choose and interpret common Incoterms, including where risk and costs pass from seller to buyer
Draft key contract clauses, SLAs with service credits and liquidated damages, and calculate what they pay

cards.title: Eighteen percent, or else
cards.setting: Noor's boardroom, Gulberg. Imran Butt arrives at 10 am with his sales manager.

lines.text: Farah sahiba, I have supplied Noor for nine years. Resin is up, the rupee is down. PKR 590 a kilo from next month, up from 500. Otherwise I cannot guarantee supply for the new plant.
(whispering) If he stops, Sheikhupura cannot start. Just agree something.
We value the partnership, Imran sahib. Let us study your figures and meet again on Thursday.
(after he leaves) He's anchoring high and using the start-up date as pressure. But we qualified the second maker last month.
Then before Thursday we need three numbers: what the price should be, what our alternative costs, and where we walk away.
Stage four: the Negotiation Table. Prepare like a professional, and then write it into a contract that holds.

scenes.heading: BATNA
scenes.narration: Your best alternative to a negotiated agreement is what you will do if this deal fails. A strong, real alternative is your greatest source of power. Improve it before you negotiate.

scenes.heading: Walk-away point
scenes.narration: Your reservation point is the worst deal you will accept, usually set by your BATNA. Decide it before the meeting, not in the heat of it.

scenes.heading: ZOPA
scenes.narration: The zone of possible agreement is the overlap between the most the buyer will pay and the least the seller will accept. No overlap, no deal, unless you create new value.

scenes.heading: Anchoring
scenes.narration: The first credible number tends to pull the final result towards it. Open with a well-supported figure, and when the other side anchors high, re-anchor with evidence rather than splitting the difference.

scenes.heading: Trade, don't give
scenes.narration: Every concession should buy something back. Use the phrase: if you do this, then we can do that. Look behind positions to interests: cash flow, volume, certainty.

cards.title: Thursday's numbers
cards.caption: Bilal and Zainab's preparation sheet, PKR per kg of film.

items.label: Current price
items.detail: Price for the last 12 months.

items.label: Imran's anchor
items.detail: An 18% increase, opened first.

items.label: Should-cost estimate
items.detail: About 10.8% increase, based on the film's cost breakdown.

items.label: BATNA: second maker
items.detail: Qualified supplier's quote; sets Noor's walk-away at 570.

cards.title: Should-cost: knowing what the price ought to be
cards.body:
A **should-cost** model breaks a price into its cost drivers and moves each by its own index.

Bilal's estimate of Kohsar's film price:

| Element | Share of price | Change | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| Resin | 60% | +15% | +9.0% |
| Conversion (energy, labour) | 30% | +6% | +1.8% |
| Overheads and margin | 10% | 0% | 0% |
| **Total** | | | **+10.8%** |

So a fair new price is about **500 x 1.108 = PKR 554/kg**, not 590.

This gives Farah a credible **counter-anchor**: evidence, not emotion. It also suggests a better long-term fix: a **price adjustment clause** that moves the resin portion with a published resin index, so neither side has to fight every quarter.

cards.question: Noor will pay at most PKR 570/kg (its walk-away, set by its BATNA). Bilal estimates Kohsar would accept no less than PKR 535/kg. What is the ZOPA?
options: PKR 500 to 535
PKR 535 to 570
PKR 570 to 590
There is no ZOPA
cards.explanation: The ZOPA runs from the seller's minimum (535) to the buyer's maximum (570). Any deal must land in that range. Noor's aim is to settle as close to 535 as it can, using evidence and traded concessions.

cards.back: A position is what someone says they want ('590 or nothing'). An interest is why ('my resin costs rose and my bank wants faster cash'). Deals are found in interests.
Responding to an extreme first offer with your own well-evidenced figure, rather than negotiating from their number.
Meeting halfway between offers. It rewards whoever anchored more aggressively, so avoid it as a default.
'If you hold the price for 12 months, then we can commit 70% of our volume.' Nothing is given without something back.
Qualifying a second source, checking import options or adjusting stock before the talks, so you need the deal less.
Distributive: dividing a fixed amount (price). Integrative: adding value both sides want, such as volume, terms or forecasts.

cards.title: Prepare the negotiation
cards.prompt: Put Farah's preparation steps for Thursday in order.
steps: Gather facts: cost breakdown, market indices, the supplier's position
Build the should-cost estimate and price the BATNA (the second maker's quote)
Set Noor's target price and walk-away point, and estimate the supplier's likely minimum
List tradeable items and what each is worth to both sides
Plan the opening offer, roles and the agenda for the meeting

cards.title: Thursday at the table
cards.situation: Imran repeats: 'PKR 590, or I may have to prioritise other customers.' Farah shows the should-cost sheet. He says his resin costs rose more than the index and that his bank is pressing him for cash. Tariq passes you a note: 'Just offer 570 and finish this.' What is your best move?

choices.text: Offer 570 now to secure supply for the start-up.
choices.outcome: Imran accepts instantly, which tells you he would have taken less. You jumped to your walk-away point and left up to PKR 35/kg on the table: millions a year.

choices.text: Propose meeting halfway between 554 and 590, at 572.
choices.outcome: It sounds fair, but it rewards his inflated anchor and lands above your own walk-away. Splitting the difference is not a strategy.

choices.text: Re-anchor at 548 with the evidence, then trade: if he accepts a resin-index price clause and 554 or less, Noor commits 70% of volume and pays in 30 days instead of 60.
choices.outcome: You address his real interest (cash flow) at little cost to Noor and keep the price near should-cost. Imran settles at 550 with an index clause. Both sides leave with something they value.

choices.text: Tell him Noor will move all volume to the second maker unless he accepts 535.
choices.outcome: The threat is partly real, which helps, but an ultimatum on a strategic supplier during start-up risks a damaging stand-off. Use the BATNA as quiet strength, not a blunt weapon.

cards.title: From handshake to contract
cards.setting: Procurement floor, Friday morning. Tea and a marked-up draft contract.

lines.text: Done: PKR 550 a kilo, resin index clause reviewed quarterly, 70% of volume, 30-day payment. And the second maker gets 30%.
Against 590 that is PKR 40 a kilo. On roughly 2,600 tonnes a year, about PKR 104 million a year saved.
A handshake is not a contract. If his deliveries slip during start-up, what happens? If we import resin-based film as backup, who carries the risk at sea?
And the 3PL contract needs teeth. If dispatch is late, my trucks wait and my product sits.
Then today we write clauses, Incoterms, service levels and damages. Let's go.

cards.title: Incoterms basics
cards.body:
**Incoterms** are standard trade terms published by the International Chamber of Commerce (current edition: 2020). Each rule says **where delivery happens**, so where **risk** passes, and **who pays** which costs.

- **EXW:** buyer collects at the seller's premises and handles almost everything.
- **FCA:** seller hands goods, export-cleared, to the buyer's carrier at a named place.
- **FOB:** seller loads goods on board the vessel at the port of shipment; risk passes there.
- **CIF:** seller pays freight and minimum insurance to the destination port, but **risk still passes when goods are on board** at origin.
- **DAP:** seller delivers at the named destination, ready to unload; buyer pays import duties.
- **DDP:** seller delivers and also pays import duties and taxes.

FOB, CFR and CIF are for sea and inland waterway. For **containers** handed over at an inland terminal, FCA, CPT or CIP usually fit better. Incoterms do **not** decide price, payment or when ownership passes: the contract must.

cards.title: The Incoterms ladder: seller's duties grow
cards.caption: Moving down the ladder, the seller takes on more cost and risk.

items.label: EXW
items.detail: Goods made available at the seller's premises. Minimum seller duty.

items.label: FCA
items.detail: Seller hands export-cleared goods to the buyer's carrier at a named place.

items.label: FOB
items.detail: Seller loads goods on board at the port of shipment; risk passes there.

items.label: CIF / CIP
items.detail: Seller also pays main freight and insurance; risk still passes at origin.

items.label: DAP
items.detail: Seller delivers at the destination, ready to unload; buyer clears import.

items.label: DDP
items.detail: Seller delivers and pays import duties and taxes. Maximum seller duty.

cards.title: Match the Incoterm
cards.prompt: Match each Incoterm to the situation in Noor's import file.

pairs.right: Noor's agent collects the culture from the producer's factory gate and arranges export clearance too
The Chinese mill loads film on board at Shanghai; from then, transit risk is Noor's
The seller pays sea freight and minimum insurance to Karachi, but risk passed at loading
The seller delivers to Noor's Sheikhupura gate; Noor clears customs and pays duties
The seller delivers to Sheikhupura and pays the import duties and taxes

cards.question: Noor buys backup film from China on FOB Shanghai terms. A container falls into the sea during the voyage to Karachi. Who bears the risk of the loss?
options: The Chinese seller
Noor, the buyer
The shipping line automatically
The Karachi port authority
cards.explanation: Under FOB, risk passes to the buyer once the goods are on board the vessel at the port of shipment. Noor bears the loss and should have arranged cargo insurance; any claim against the carrier depends on the transport contract.

cards.title: What does each clause do?
cards.prompt: Sort the clauses in the draft film and 3PL contracts by their main purpose.

items.text: Liquidated damages for late delivery
SLA: 98% of orders dispatched on time each month
Quarterly resin-index price adjustment
Payment within 30 days of a matched invoice
Force majeure for events beyond either party's control
Termination for repeated failure after written notice
Arbitration in Lahore before going to court
Acceptance testing of each film batch against the specification

items.label: Used for
items.left: Late completion or delivery, mostly in supply and project contracts
items.right: Ongoing services measured against service levels

items.label: How set
items.left: A pre-agreed sum per day or week of delay, with a cap
items.right: A percentage of the period's fee for each missed target

items.label: Basis
items.left: A genuine pre-estimate of the buyer's likely loss
items.right: A price adjustment for service below the agreed level

items.label: Watch out
items.left: A sum far above any real loss looks like a penalty
items.right: Credits that are too small are cheaper to pay than to perform

cards.title: Putting numbers on the teeth
cards.body:
**Film supply for start-up (LDs):** contract value PKR 24m. LDs of **0.5% of contract value per week** of delay, capped at **10%**.

- 3 weeks late: 24m x 0.5% x 3 = **PKR 360,000**
- Cap: 24m x 10% = PKR 2.4m, reached after 20 weeks; beyond that, Noor relies on termination rights.

**3PL services (service credits):** monthly fee PKR 3.2m. Target: **98%** on-time dispatch. Credit of **2% of the monthly fee for each full percentage point below target**, capped at 10% a month.
